title: Dharma is subtle
hook: a king objects to his daughter's marriage, and the answer is that dharma is subtle
carry: dharma is subtle: hard cases need honest questions
tomorrow: Fear not: Maya spared from the fire

segments.voice: Yesterday, Draupadi's swayamvara came home: Kunti's word, given without looking, and kept with care. Your line was satya: even a careless word is kept true.

Drupada has a problem. His daughter was won by a brahmin no one could name, and now he learns who the man really is: Arjuna, alive, the one he'd hoped for from the start. Good news. Then Yudhishthira tells him the rest. Draupadi will be the wife of all five brothers. Drupada objects at once. One woman with many husbands, he says, is not the way of the Vedas or of custom. How can you, who know what's right, propose this?

Yudhishthira answers carefully. Dharma is subtle, he says, and its path is hard to see. He follows where those before him walked, and his mother has spoken. Then Vyasa arrives, and Drupada asks him directly: is this right, or not? Vyasa takes Drupada aside and tells him a story. In an earlier life, your daughter was a sage's daughter who couldn't find a husband. She practiced hard austerities, and Shiva came to grant her a wish. Give me a husband, she asked, again and again. And Shiva told her: since you asked more than once, in another birth you'll have more than one husband. Vyasa tells a second story too, of the brothers as gods born on earth, and Drupada is persuaded. Now the teaching, in Yudhishthira's first words: dharma is subtle. The Mahabharata says it again and again; it's one of the epic's big ideas. Dharma, the right way, isn't always a rule you look up. Sometimes good rules pull against each other: a mother's word, a father's custom, brothers who mustn't be divided. So the poem doesn't hide the hard case. It lets Drupada object out loud that this isn't the custom, and it gives four reasons, not one. And Draupadi herself says almost nothing here; her voice comes later, and it's fierce. Hindus have argued over this marriage ever since. That's how the epic teaches: with cases hard enough to make you ask.
screen: `DHARMA IS SUBTLE.` · `VYASA'S STORY OF ANOTHER LIFE.` · `GOOD RULES THAT PULL APART.` · `FOUR REASONS, AND ONE SILENCE.` · then, large: `CASES HARD ENOUGH TO MAKE YOU ASK.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind a hard question in your own family or faith, one where two good things pull against each other. Don't solve it. Hold both sides, the way the poem holds Drupada's objection and Yudhishthira's answer, and then ask who hasn't been heard yet. If you pray, ask for clear sight; if you don't, just let the question stay open a little longer.
Draupadi's swayamvara. Its last piece: Drupada's objection, Yudhishthira's answer, and Vyasa's story of a wish asked more than once.
Your line: dharma is subtle: hard cases need honest questions. Four answers, and the poem still lets you ask. That's the swayamvara, start to finish.

howItsDone: Draupadi's marriage is discussed in Hindu teaching and retelling; some retellings lean on Vyasa's account of her past life, and some modern novels tell the whole Mahabharata from Draupadi's side.

notes: All paraphrase. Confirm in Ganguli: Drupada's objection (against usage and the Vedas); Yudhishthira's 'dharma is subtle' answer and his appeal to precedent and to his mother's word.
